| rule.ch00.1-what-blend65.blend65-statically-typed-compiled-programming-language | [spec/00-introduction.md](../spec/00-introduction.md) | &#91;"Chapter 00 — Introduction &amp; Design Axioms","1. What Is Blend65?"&#93; | Blend65 is a statically typed, compiled programming language for the MOS 6502 CPU family. It targets retro computing platforms where every byte of RAM, every CPU cycle, and every page of ROM matters. The language provides a modern, C-like development experience while generating machine code that meets the hard real-time and memory constraints of 8-bit hardware. | sha256:26ee70f38932580e4797978dabddb82247f790ab0b84487b3d87aa1681f37e62 | 11 | Blend65 is a statically typed, compiled programming language for the MOS 6502 CPU family. | mandatory-c64 | &#91;"compiler-api"&#93; | &#91;&#93; | &#91;&#93; |

| rule.ch00.a3-no-undefined-behavior.deliberate-design-choice-blend65-not-auto | [spec/00-introduction.md](../spec/00-introduction.md) | &#91;"Chapter 00 — Introduction &amp; Design Axioms","3. Design Axioms","A3 — No Undefined Behavior"&#93; | **Unspecified values are not undefined behavior.** A variable declared without an initializer (→ Ch 03, VAR-2) holds an **unspecified value** — whatever bytes already occupied that RAM, zero-page, or register location. Reading it is fully defined: it yields *some* valid value of the variable's type, of the correct width, with no other effect. The value is simply not *predictable*. This is a deliberate design choice — Blend65 does not auto-zero variables at startup, because doing so would cost cycles and bytes that the target hardware cannot spare. | rule.ch02.1-overview.blend65-v3-fully-explicitly-typed-variable | [spec/02-type-system.md](../spec/02-type-system.md) | &#91;"Chapter 02 — Type System","1. Overview"&#93; | Blend65 v3 is **fully explicitly typed** — every variable, constant, parameter, and return type requires an explicit type annotation. There is no type inference. This is a deliberate design choice: on the 6502, the difference between `byte` and `word` directly determines memory usage, register allocation, and cycle counts. Overview"&#93; | An enum defines a **named set of byte-sized constants** under a single named type. Overview"&#93; | Under SFA, an enum has **zero runtime cost** — each member is a compile-time `byte` constant, and an enum-typed variable occupies exactly one byte of storage.
